analysis.one_liner: Slashes the top tax rate on investment profits to 15% and adjusts asset values for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action in the Senate and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten how the tax code treats profits from selling stocks, businesses, and property. It would have cut the top tax rate on long-term investment gains from the ordinary income rate down to 15%, adjusted the purchase price of assets upward for inflation before taxing the profit, and given a special 20% top rate plus a large deduction for profits on small-business stock. It was introduced by Senator William Armstrong with three Republican cosponsors and was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who sell stocks and other assets at a profit — a group skewed toward higher-income households — would pay sharply less tax. People holding assets for years would also avoid being taxed on gains that are just inflation. Holders of small-business stock would get an additional 28.5% deduction, and corporations a 41% deduction, on those profits.

how_it_helps.text: Allows individuals a deduction equal to 46.4% of long-term capital gains, which cuts the effective top rate on those gains to 15%, for sales before 1991 [S2] [S3].

Requires indexing: for assets held more than a year and sold after 1990, the purchase price is multiplied by the growth in the gross national product deflator, so inflation is not taxed as profit [S2] [S3].
Gives noncorporate taxpayers a 28.5% deduction on gains from small-business stock held at least four years, with a 20% maximum rate, and gives corporations a 41% deduction on such gains [S2] [S3].
Sponsors and supporters of such measures argue lower capital gains taxes encourage investment in new businesses, which is why the bill includes targeted small-business stock provisions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would collect less revenue from asset sales, meaning either other taxes stay higher, services are cut, or deficits grow. Because capital gains are heavily concentrated among high-income households, the tax savings would flow overwhelmingly to them.

drawbacks.text: The bill undoes a core deal of the 1986 Tax Reform Act, which had eliminated the capital gains preference in exchange for lower overall rates; restoring it reopens the gap between tax on work and tax on investment profits [S2] [S3].

The bill would go further than the small-business break for the whole market: the 15% rate and inflation indexing apply to all capital gains, not just gains from startups, so the largest benefits go to holders of large existing stock portfolios [S2] [S3].

The bill itself acknowledges the revenue cost by adding the new small-business deduction to the alternative minimum tax's preference items, a recognition that the deductions are large enough to require a minimum-tax backstop [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The small-business stock provisions are the most defensible part: they target new investment in young companies. But most of the bill — the 15% rate and inflation indexing — is an across-the-board cut on gains from all assets, concentrated among the wealthiest households, paid for through forgone federal revenue that everyone else ultimately covers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Finance Committee in July 1989, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator William Armstrong (R-CO) introduced the bill on July 13, 1989, with Senators Symms and Boschwitz, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee [S1] [S3] [S5].
Three Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber [S5].
The bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the treatment of capital gains stayed as written in the 1986 Tax Reform Act, and the Treasury kept the revenue the bill would have forgiven — a cost that would otherwise have been spread to general taxpayers.

for.name: Sen. William L. Armstrong
for.role: U.S. Senator from Colorado; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the capital gains rate to 15%, index asset bases for inflation, and create small-business stock deductions.

for.name: Sens. Steven Symms and Rudy Boschwitz
for.role: U.S. Senators from Idaho and Minnesota; cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside the sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died in committee at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never scheduled the bill for consideration; the bill received no committee action after its July 1989 referral.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so the partisan split was never tested; the sponsor and all three cosponsors were Republicans, and no action by Democrats is recorded beyond the committee's inaction [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Would cut the top rate on investment profits to 15% and stop taxing inflation as gain, savings concentrated among households with large portfolios. The cost is forgone federal revenue borne by general taxpayers.

A 28.5% deduction and 20% top rate on profits from small-business stock held four years would directly boost returns for startup backers. A similar benefit for people who need startups is indirect at best.
Corporations would get a 41% deduction on gains from qualified small-business stock, and a 20% maximum corporate rate on such gains, making equity fundraising for qualifying companies cheaper.

Lower taxes on asset sales increase the payoff to trading, holding, and managing capital gains assets, expanding business for brokerages and fund managers. The public cost is the revenue the Treasury gives up.
